sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Software engineering (SE) is the art and science of building software — not just writing code, but doing so deliberately, reliably, and at team scale. The unit opens with a blunt claim: SE centres around coding, yet coding can go badly wrong without everything around it.

Why does that matter for your midterm? Because nearly every planning question is really asking: can you show the engineering around the code — the plans, estimates, graphs and trade-offs that keep a project honest?

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: Programming is crucial to SE, but SE is more than programming. The lecture lists what the rest looks like: co-ordinating a team and managing the project, understanding user requirements, designing components, implementing them, testing piece by piece, verifying the software meets its goals, and maintaining it afterwards.

Whole books have been written about each of these, and every company does them differently — there is no one-size-fits-all approach. That sentence is worth remembering: examiners reward answers that adapt a technique to the situation rather than reciting one true method.

sections.heading: Why software is hard to build
bullets: It has no physical size — you cannot see or feel it, so progress is invisible without explicit models (graphs, backlogs, charts).
Customers often do not know what they want, so requirements must be elicited, not just collected.
Failures hide: you need to know when something goes wrong and how to fix it without breaking the rest.
Coordination overhead grows with team size; communication is part of the product.
Time estimation is structurally uncertain — which is why this unit spends so much time on estimation techniques.
paras: The lecture's challenge slide frames all of this as open questions, and the course answers each one with a concrete tool: WBS answers what to build, planning poker answers how long, activity graphs answer in what order, burn-up charts answer are we on track.

sections.heading: Exam relevance

callout.text: Definitions of SE and 'why is SE more than programming' appear as short-answer warm-ups. Answer with the activity list plus one consequence (cost overrun, lawsuit, lost data) to show you grasp the stakes, not just the vocabulary.

paras: Short-answer questions love this topic because it is easy to mark: list the activities, explain one challenge, connect it to a technique from later in the unit.

summary: Software engineering is the disciplined art of building software at team scale: coding plus planning, requirements, design, testing, verification and maintenance.
title: Software engineering: more than programming

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: A software development lifecycle (SDLC) model is a broad strategy for organising a project: which phases happen, in what order, and how you handle the discovery that something earlier was wrong. The lecture presents three classic answers — iterative waterfall, spiral, and prototyping — and the 2022 midterm asked students to explain the first from scratch.

sections.heading: The iterative waterfall
paras: Phases (requirements, design, coding/debugging, and onward) run in sequence, but with feedback loops: when a later phase uncovers a problem, you step back and rework the earlier phase before proceeding. That single sentence is essentially the 4-mark answer the 2022 paper wanted, plus one consequence.

The consequence examiners look for: late changes are expensive, because rework cascades through every phase built on top of the faulty one. Faulty requirements discovered during testing can mean redesigning, recoding and retesting — which is exactly why later lectures obsess over getting requirements right early.

sections.heading: The spiral model
paras: The spiral divides the timeline into cycles, each with four parts: determine objectives and options, identify and resolve risks, develop and verify, then plan the next cycle. Risk mitigation is the entire point — the model suits projects where the biggest danger is building the wrong thing or hitting an unknown technical wall.
Think of it as the waterfall curled around a risk compass: each loop around the spiral buys down uncertainty before committing more money.

sections.heading: Prototyping
paras: A prototype is a quick, deliberately incomplete piece of work built to answer a question — what the interface could feel like, whether a technical approach works. Throwaway prototypes are discarded; evolutionary ones grow into the product. The exam trap is calling any unfinished program a prototype: a prototype must have a question it is trying to answer.

sections.heading: How to choose (and how to answer)

head: Situation
Fitting model
Why
rows: Sequential phases with limited feedback are cheapest when surprises are unlikely
High risk, large or novel system
Each cycle explicitly attacks the biggest remaining risk

callout.text: 2022 Midterm B Q1.1 asked for the iterative waterfall in 4 marks: 1 for phase order, 1 for feedback loops, 1 for an example of stepping back, 1 for the cost-of-change consequence. Structure every 'explain a model' answer that way.

summary: Lifecycle models organise a project: iterative waterfall sequences phases with feedback, spiral cycles around risk, and prototypes answer open questions cheaply.
title: Lifecycle models: waterfall, spiral, prototyping

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: A work breakdown structure (WBS) is divide-and-conquer applied to project management: break the project into tasks, break big tasks into subtasks, stop before the detail becomes noise. Everything downstream — estimates, graphs, critical paths, Gantt charts — eats the WBS as its input, so a sloppy WBS poisons the whole plan.

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: A WBS lists activities hierarchically (e.g. game project: market research, prototyping, game design split into core concepts, background story, and so on). Two annotations make it plannable: dependencies, which state that some tasks must finish before others start, and milestones, which mark significant achievements rather than work itself.

Dependencies are usually shown in a task table: activity, duration, depends-on. The 2022 midterm handed students exactly such a table (Project A, tasks A-H with durations and dependencies) and asked for a graph, earliest/latest times and the critical path — all mechanically derived from the WBS.

sections.heading: Worked example
paras: Worksheet 1 makes you build one for a train line between two universities or a music festival on an island resort — deliberately unfamiliar domains, so you practise decomposing rather than reciting. The worked pattern:

1. Brainstorm major deliverables (route survey, demolition, track laying, electrification, stations...). 2. Decompose each once or twice — station construction splits into foundations, platforms, roofing. 3. Add a dependencies column using activity numbers. 4. Sanity-check: every task has an owner-able size (days to weeks), and nothing important lacks a predecessor.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: A WBS is not a schedule: it says what depends on what, not when anything happens. Dates come later via graphs and Gantt charts.
More detail is not always better: tasks estimated at 0, infinity or '?' in planning poker signal a WBS item that needs splitting or clarifying.
Milestones are not tasks: 'track tested' is a milestone; 'test track' is the task that earns it.

callout.text: If handed a WBS task table in the exam, first rewrite it cleanly with columns Task / Duration / Dependencies, then draw the graph. Most lost marks come from misread dependencies, not from the graph algorithm.

summary: A work breakdown structure decomposes a project into tasks with dependencies and milestones — the raw material for every schedule that follows.
title: Work breakdown structures

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Estimation matters because time is money: in software you spend on people and their time, so a duration estimate is a cost estimate wearing a different hat. The lecture surveys three approaches — expert models (COCOMO), task-by-task judgement, and planning poker — and lands firmly on the last for real teamwork.

sections.heading: COCOMO and its problem
paras: COCOMO, the COnstructive COst MOdel, estimates effort and schedule from program size calibrated against historical data. The lecture's warning is memorable: lies, damned lies and statistics. A model fitted to other organisations' past projects produces precise-looking numbers whose assumptions may not hold for yours. Useful as a sanity check; dangerous as a promise.

sections.heading: Real-world estimation is task-by-task
paras: In practice, teams estimate each WBS activity individually and add them up through the network (which is why the critical path, not the sum of all tasks, sets the project duration). The hard part is honesty: individuals anchor on the first number spoken aloud, and optimists hide uncertainty. Planning poker is a social protocol designed to defeat exactly those failure modes.

sections.heading: How it works: planning poker
paras: Each estimator holds cards 0, 1/2, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100, '?' and infinity. For each task, everyone plays a card face down, then all reveal at once. Matching cards mean consensus — record it and move on. Divergent cards mean someone knows something: the highest and lowest estimators explain their reasoning, the team discusses what the task really involves, and you re-estimate.

The Fibonacci-like spread is deliberate: near-identical small numbers are distinguishable (1 vs 2 days matters), while large numbers blur together (40 vs 100 both mean 'big and uncertain — split this task'). Infinity and '?' are legitimate bids meaning 'too big to estimate' or 'I don't understand the task' — both trigger decomposition, not embarrassment. The worked examples in the slides show a 3-person team converging on a task estimate, then hitting triple-digit cards on '4.2 Coding' and splitting the task instead of budgeting 100 days.

sections.heading: Exam relevance

callout.text: Worksheet 2 Q1(b) asks where planning poker fits in Scrum: estimation of backlog items / sprint planning. Worksheet 1 Q2 tests the mechanics. Always mention simultaneous reveal (anti-anchoring) and discuss-then-re-estimate — those two moves earn the marks.

paras: Estimation questions also hide inside burn-up chart problems: planned progress per day equals the sum of task durations divided by planned project duration (2022 Q4: 200/100 = 2 days of effort per day).

summary: Estimation turns WBS tasks into durations: COCOMO models from history (handle with care), real teams estimate task-by-task, and planning poker defeats anchoring through simultaneous reveal and discussion.
title: Estimation and planning poker

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Task tables are easy to write but hard to reason about: a list of dependencies does not show the shape of the project. Activity graphs turn the WBS task table into a network you can compute over — the foundation for earliest/latest times, slack, the critical path, and the Gantt chart. Every midterm in the archive asks students to draw one.

sections.heading: Activity-on-node (AON)
paras: Each activity is a node (box) labelled with its name and duration; each arrow means 'must finish before'. If B depends on A, draw A → B. The 2022 paper's Project A (A:3; B:5 and C:6 and D:10 after A; E:4 after B,C; F:3 after C,D; G:5 after E,F; H:4 after G) becomes a diamond-lattice flowing A → {B,C,D} → {E,F} → G → H. The 2019 paper tested the same skill with seven tasks.

For timing analysis each node later carries four numbers — earliest start/finish and latest start/finish — computed by forward and backward passes (see the critical path article). Different textbooks arrange the four numbers differently; any consistent layout the lectures accept is fine, but keep yours legible under exam pressure.

sections.heading: Activity-on-arc (AOA)
paras: Each activity is an arrow; nodes are events (moments in time). The 2018 paper asked for AOA explicitly. AOA's awkwardness is the dummy task: a zero-duration arrow sometimes needed when two activities share only part of their dependencies. The slides' game-dev example needs dummies around testing tasks (functionality testing, playability testing, coding, artwork) to keep the logic exact.
Exam tactic: use whichever form the question names. If it says 'activity graph, your choice' (Worksheet 1 Q4), pick AON — no dummies, fewer ways to lose marks.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: Arrows mean dependency ('must complete before'), not the passage of time and not data flow.
AOA nodes are instants, not work: never put durations on AOA nodes.
A use-case diagram is not an activity graph (the Lecture 3 slides warn about this confusion explicitly).

callout.text: Graph-drawing marks reward completeness: every task present, every dependency shown, durations labelled. Draw nodes large enough for the four timing numbers you will add in the next question part.

summary: Activity graphs make dependencies computable: AON puts work on nodes, AOA puts work on arrows (with occasional dummy tasks) — both feed timing analysis.
title: Activity graphs: AON and AOA

recall.a: Forward pass: ES = max(EF of predecessors), EF = ES + duration. Project duration = max EF. Backward pass: LF = min(LS of successors), LS = LF - duration. Slack = LS - ES.
recall.q: Recite the forward/backward pass rules and the slack formula.

recall.a: It has zero slack; delaying any of its activities delays the whole project. Crash it (add resources) or fast-track it, and protect it first.
recall.q: Why does management care about the critical path?

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: The critical path is the longest chain through the activity network — and therefore the shortest time the project can possibly take. The 2022 midterm devoted 11 of its 25 planning marks to computing earliest/latest times, slack, and the critical path from a task table, so this is the single highest-yield calculation in the unit.

sections.heading: How it works: the two passes
paras: Assume the project starts at day (or week) 0. Forward pass: each activity's earliest start (ES) is the maximum earliest finish (EF) of its predecessors; its EF is ES plus its own duration. The project's estimated duration is the maximum EF across all activities.

Backward pass: each activity's latest finish (LF) is the minimum latest start (LS) of its successors (end activities take LF equal to the project duration); its LS is LF minus duration. Slack (float) is LS minus ES — equivalently LF minus EF — the time an activity can slip without delaying the project.

sections.heading: Worked example (2022 Project A)
paras: Forward pass: A finishes at 3; B ends 8, C ends 9, D ends 13; E starts at max(8,9)=9 and ends 13; F starts at max(9,13)=13 and ends 16; G ends 21; H ends 25. Project duration: 25 weeks.

Backward pass from 25: H(21-25), G(16-21), F(13-16), E(10-14), D(3-13), C(3-9), B(9-14), A(0-3). Slack activities: B (6 weeks) and E (1 week). Critical path: A → C → D? No — check edges: F needs C and D; G needs E and F. Zero-slack chain: A → D → F → G → H (3+10+3+5+4 = 25 ✓), with C also zero-slack feeding F. So the critical paths are A-C-F-G-H (21? 3+6+3+5+4=21 ✗ — not critical!). Recheck: C: ES 3, EF 9, LF 13? F starts at 13 (needs D's 13), so C's LF = 13-3... wait C duration 6, LS = 13-6 = 7? Let me redo carefully: F LS: LF 16 - 3 = 13. C: successor F (LS 13) → LF 13, LS 7, slack 4. D: successor F (LS 13) → LF 13, LS 3, slack 0. E: successor G (LS 16) → LF 16, LS 12, slack 3. B: successor E (LS 12) → LF 12, LS 7, slack 4. A: successors B (LS 7), C (LS 7), D (LS 3) → LF 3, LS 0, slack 0. Critical path: A → D → F → G → H = 3+10+3+5+4 = 25 ✓. Slack: B 4, C 4, E 3. (This correction is exactly why you always verify path sums equal the duration — do the same in the exam.)

sections.heading: Using it to manage
paras: The 2022 paper's final planning part asks why critical path and slack are managerially useful (3 marks): the critical path tells you which activities cannot slip without moving the deadline — crash these (add resources) or fast-track them first; slack tells you where resources can be borrowed from without harm, and where contingency can hide. Monitoring the critical path is monitoring the deadline.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: The critical path is the longest path, not the shortest: 'critical' means delay-critical.
There can be more than one critical path; delaying any of them delays the project.
Slack belongs to paths, shared across activities: using one activity's slack consumes its neighbours'.
Duration is not the sum of all tasks: tasks off the critical path overlap in time.

callout.text: Always verify: at least one zero-slack chain must sum exactly to the project duration. If none does, your backward pass has an error — recheck successor lists before moving on.

summary: Forward pass gives earliest times and duration; backward pass gives latest times; slack is their difference; the zero-slack chain is the critical path that sets the deadline.
title: Critical path and slack time

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: A Gantt chart turns the network analysis into a calendar: each activity becomes a horizontal bar positioned at its scheduled start and ending at its finish. Where activity graphs answer 'what depends on what', Gantt charts answer 'who does what, when' — the artefact you would actually pin to the lab wall.

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: Rows list activities; the horizontal axis is time. Bar position encodes the ES/EF schedule (or the LS schedule if you want to show how late things may start). Multi-colour Gantt charts are common: colours can distinguish teams, phases, or critical vs non-critical activities so the deadline-drivers jump out.

The lecture closes the planning arc here: WBS decomposes, poker estimates, graphs order, critical-path analysis times, and the Gantt chart communicates. An exam question that says 'present your plan' usually wants this final translation step, not another network diagram.

sections.heading: PERT in one paragraph
paras: The additional-notes slides introduce PERT estimation: instead of one estimate per task, collect optimistic, most-likely and pessimistic estimates and combine them (expected = (O + 4M + P)/6). Use it when uncertainty is high enough that a single number would be fiction — and say so explicitly to earn method marks.

summary: Gantt charts communicate the schedule as bars on a timeline; PERT refines estimates under uncertainty with three-point weighted averages.
title: Gantt charts and PERT

sections.heading: How planning marks are lost
bullets: Misreading the dependency table (especially multi-predecessor tasks like E after B,C).
Drawing the graph without durations, then having nowhere to put ES/EF/LS/LF.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Lecture 2 is titled 'From Planning to Doing': the plan exists, now how do teams execute it without the plan fossilising? The lecture draws a line students often blur — lifecycle models (waterfall, spiral) are broad organising strategies, while processes (Scrum, Lean, Kanban-flavoured workflows) are the concrete ways teams run the work day to day.

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: Agile methods replace one big delivery with a series of short iterations (the lecture names 1–4-week sprints). Each iteration creates something concrete and useful for the customer, even if small, and the client stays closely involved throughout — scope and priorities are renegotiated rather than frozen.

That involvement is the point: when even your customer doesn't know what they want (Lecture 1's challenge), short feedback loops beat long specifications. Tools for obtaining requirements therefore shift too — user stories and backlogs replace big upfront documents, and progress is monitored with burn-up charts and Kanban boards rather than only Gantt charts.

sections.heading: Exam relevance

callout.text: Worksheet 2 Q1(c) asks how Scrum handles mid-project requirement changes and who is responsible — the signature agile-vs-waterfall question. Answer: reprioritise the backlog via the Product Owner; the sprint itself stays protected.

paras: Expect compare-and-contrast prompts: traditional SE negotiates scope upfront (faulty requirements are expensive to fix late), agile embraces changing requirements through reprioritisation.

summary: Agile delivers in short client-involved iterations; lifecycle models organise, processes execute — Scrum, backlogs, burn-ups and Kanban are this lecture's toolkit.
title: From planning to doing: agile processes

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Scrum is the agile process this unit teaches in depth: small self-managing teams, time-boxed sprints, and three accountabilities with sharply separated jobs. It appears in Worksheet 2 Q1, in the 2022 midterm Q4.3-4, and in the ethics handout's social-media scenario — making it one of the most examined topics in the course.

sections.heading: The three accountabilities

head: Role
Job in one line
Owns
rows: Product Owner (one person, not a committee)
Maximises value; owns content and ordering of the Product Backlog
Turn backlog items into a usable Increment each sprint
The Sprint Backlog plan and quality
Protects the process; removes barriers between stakeholders and team

paras: The team as a whole is cross-functional (all skills needed each sprint) and self-managing (members decide internally who does what, when and how). Examiners test this: a common trap answer has the Scrum Master assigning tasks — wrong; the team self-manages.

sections.heading: How it handles change
paras: Mid-project requirement changes go through the Product Owner into the Product Backlog, and are taken up in future sprints — never by interrupting the current sprint. That protected time-box plus reprioritised backlog is the whole agile answer to changing requirements, and it is exactly what Worksheet 2 Q1(c) asks for.

sections.heading: Planning poker meets Scrum
paras: Worksheet 2 Q1(b) asks where planning poker fits: estimation of Product Backlog items, typically during backlog refinement and sprint planning, so the team commits only to what it believes it can finish.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: Scrum Master is not a manager: no task assignment, no command authority.
Product Owner is exactly one person: committees diffuse the priority call.
Changing requirements mid-sprint is not agile: agility lives in backlog reprioritisation between sprints.

summary: Scrum: one Product Owner owns priorities, Developers build each sprint's increment, the Scrum Master protects the process — change flows through the backlog, never into an active sprint.
title: Scrum framework and roles

sections.heading: The two backlogs
paras: The Product Backlog is the single ordered list of everything that might go into the product — features, fixes, knowledge work — owned and ordered by the Product Owner, evolving as requirements change. The Sprint Backlog is the Developers' plan for one sprint: the Sprint Goal (why), the selected Product Backlog items (what), and the delivery plan (how). Once the sprint starts, its backlog is the team's commitment, not a suggestion box.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Burn-up (earned-value) charts show the big picture: planned progress versus actual progress over time. The lecture builds them in eight explicit steps from the WBS and poker estimates, Worksheet 2 walks you through a spreadsheet of a space-visualisation project, and the 2022 midterm tested the arithmetic cold. Learn the recipe once and all three fall into place.

sections.heading: How it works: the construction recipe
paras: Step 1: from the WBS and planning-poker estimates, list each task's estimated duration. Step 2: sum all task durations (2022: 200 days). Step 3: take the planned project duration from the network analysis (2022: 100 days). Step 4: planned progress per day = sum / duration = 200/100 = 2 days of effort per day. Step 5: planned progress at time t is rate x t (day 30 → 60). Step 6: pick the time t. Step 7: find tasks with actual finish time <= t (the SUMIF step in the worksheet). Step 8: actual progress = sum of their estimated durations.

The subtle point students miss: actual progress adds estimated durations, not actual durations — it measures earned value (how much planned work got done), which is why finishing a 20-day-estimate task in 30 days still earns 20.

sections.heading: Monitoring: scope and judgement
paras: Compare the lines: actual above planned means ahead, below means behind. Burn-up charts often add a scope line, because agile projects gain work mid-flight — rising scope with flat actuals is the classic distress signal. The worksheet's alternate-world scenario (day 40, several render tasks unfinished) asks what action you would take: replan scope, add reviewers, or renegotiate the deadline — the chart informs the decision, and the Scrum Guide reminds us no chart replaces empiricism: inspect the increment, not just the lines.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: Actual progress uses estimated durations of finished tasks, not how long they actually took.
Being 'ahead' on the chart while scope grows may still mean trouble.
The chart shows the big picture across tasks; per-task status is Kanban's job (the lecture pairs them deliberately).

callout.text: Show the SUMIF-style reasoning in words: 'tasks finished by day 30 are X (est. a), Y (est. b), so actual = a+b'. Method marks survive even if you mis-add.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: If burn-up charts are the project's satellite view, Kanban boards are the street map: every task sits in exactly one workflow column (Todo, Coding/Testing, Review, Awaiting Merge, Done), and the board shows the status of individual tasks against the workflow. The 2022 midterm and Worksheet 2 both test whether you can reason about flow — not just describe columns.

sections.heading: How it works: WIP limits
paras: A work-in-progress limit caps how many tasks may sit in a column (the worksheet scenario uses three). The limit forces finish-before-start: you cannot pull new coding work while review overflows, so bottlenecks become visible as piles instead of hiding as 'almost done'. The lecture's diagnostic is blunt: if review piles up while coding starves, you need more reviewers and fewer coders — re-balance the team, don't just hurry.
The 2-mark exam answer: WIP limits prevent overload, expose bottlenecks early, keep feedback fast, and protect quality by stopping half-finished work from accumulating.

sections.heading: Worked reasoning (worksheet scenario)
paras: With a WIP limit of three and columns full of rendering tasks, rushing 'Spacecraft Rendering' through means something else must finish first: at minimum, enough tasks must reach Done to free capacity along its path — and the worksheet pushes you to notice the number is a lower bound, because real dependencies and rework usually force more. When the client is unhappy with merged work, Kanban-correct handling is to move the card back from Done to the active column it belongs in (respecting WIP), fix, re-review and re-merge: Done means accepted by the client, not merely merged.

sections.heading: Adapting the process
paras: The worksheet's final twist adds documentation per task (written after code, then reviewed and merged): the Kanban-correct response is a new column or sub-workflow for docs with its own WIP limit, keeping the finish-before-start discipline rather than letting docs pile up unreviewed. The same thinking answers 'Kanban for studying ISE topics': columns like To Learn / Reading / Practising / Done with a WIP limit of two topics.

summary: Kanban makes task status visible against the workflow; WIP limits force finishing over starting, expose bottlenecks, and define what Done really means.
title: Kanban boards and WIP limits

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Code review sits in the Kanban Review column and inside agile iterations alike: another pair of eyes on code before it merges. The lecture treats reviews as both a quality gate and a monitoring tool — reviewers find different kinds of faults than testing does, and the review queue is itself a flow signal.

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: Lightweight peer review is the agile default: author submits, reviewer reads for defects, asks for fixes, approves. Formal software inspection (Fagan-style, with roles, preparation and logging) is heavier: justified for safety-critical or complex code, but the worksheet pushes you to argue it is a poor fit for a fast-moving visualisation tool where speed and checklist discipline matter more.

Reviews happen after coding/testing and before merge — exactly where the Kanban board puts them. A 5-8 item checklist for the worksheet's space-visualisation project mixes the universal (naming, error handling, boundary conditions, correct datatypes, rounding/epsilon handling, resource cleanup) with the project-specific (coordinate transforms, rendering resource disposal, data-file validation). Checklists help juniors and get in the way for experts — tailor depth to reviewer experience, a nuance the slides state explicitly.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: Review is not testing: reviewers reason about code, tests execute it — the two find different fault classes.
Checklists do not replace judgement: automate what can be checked automatically (style, types), spend human attention on logic.
Fixed defects re-occur: the lecture notes regressions explicitly, which is why re-review after fixes matters.

summary: Code review inspects code before merge: lightweight peer review for agile pace, formal inspection only where criticality justifies it, checklists tuned to reviewer and project.
title: Code review and inspection

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Functional requirements (FRs) describe what the system should do — its functions. The lecture's test is beautifully simple: a function transforms inputs into outputs (save file, print, make a backup). Everything else — how fast, how reliably, how usably — belongs to non-functional requirements, and the 2022 midterm opened its requirements question by demanding exactly this distinction.

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: Represent FRs with user stories (agile, lightweight) and use cases (detailed, contractual). Both are part of the Software Requirements Specification (SRS), the document listing all requirements. Requirements in traditional SE are negotiated upfront over scope; in agile they evolve iteration by iteration — but faulty requirements are expensive to fix late in either world, because design, code and tests all pile on top of them.

Changing requirements get their own lecture section for a reason: if requirements never changed, life would be easy. Since they do, you need elicitation tools (stories, cases, prototypes) plus a change strategy matched to your process.

sections.heading: SRS in miniature
paras: The lecture adapts the IEEE SRS layout: introduction (purpose, scope, definitions), overall description, external interface requirements, then functional requirements — with NFRs and supporting material alongside. You will not write a full SRS in the midterm, but questions assume you know what one contains and where each requirement type lives.

callout.text: 2022 Q3.1 (4 marks): two differences FR vs NFR. Score with: (1) do vs be, with examples; (2) representation — FRs via use cases/flows, NFRs via measurable constraints — plus a test-verb contrast (execute the function vs measure the characteristic).

summary: Functional requirements say what the system does — functions turning inputs into outputs, captured in user stories and use cases inside the SRS.
title: Functional requirements

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Before writing any requirement, ask: who cares, and who interacts? Stakeholders are everyone who cares about the software (users, clients, regulators, operators). Actors are the subset that interact with the system — and the lecture is strict about sorting them correctly, because the use-case header demands exactly one primary actor and a complete secondary cast.

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: Each use case has one primary actor, always a person: the one whose goal the use case serves (the uploader uploading, the customer ordering, User A adding a friend). Secondary actors are external systems or services the system needs to do its job — databases, payment gateways, authentication servers. Databases deserve special attention in this unit: use cases constantly read and store through an external database, so name it as a secondary actor rather than waving at 'the system'.

Some external systems are irrelevant: if the use case never touches them, they stay off the diagram and out of the header. The video-sharing example (watching, uploading, reporting videos) keeps only the externals each goal actually uses.

sections.heading: Task-level goals
paras: The system under consideration supports many goals at different levels. Task-level (user-goal) goals are the ones worth use cases: watching a video, uploading a video, plotting data. Below them sit sub-goals (choosing a file); above them sit summary goals (managing a channel). The 2022 paper's Q2.2(d) tests exactly this: name two task-level goals besides 'plot data' with their primary actors. Aim one level: too high is vague, too low is a paragraph of the flow.

summary: Stakeholders care, actors interact: one person as primary actor per use case, external systems as secondary actors, each goal pitched at task level.
title: Stakeholders, actors and goals

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: User stories are agile's tiny requirement slips: one sentence, three parts, written from the user's point of view. The 2022 midterm asked students to explain the three parts and then write two stories for a railway booking system — 6 marks for roughly two sentences, which makes this the densest mark-per-word topic in the unit.

sections.heading: The three parts
paras: As a <role>, I want <feature/goal> so that <benefit>. Role: who benefits (student, administrator, passenger — a real user, not 'the system'). Want: the goal or feature (register for pracs, book a return ticket). So-that: the reason, which justifies priority and scope (so that I don't miss out). The worksheet is explicit: all three parts must be present, and they must be in a single sentence.

Lecture example: 'As a student, I want to register for pracs so that I don't miss out.' Railway answers in the same mould: 'As a passenger, I want to book a return ticket in one transaction so that I don't have to queue twice.' Two distinct functionalities, two real roles, two real benefits — that is the full 4 marks.

sections.heading: Stories in the larger machine
paras: Each story is a task in the WBS: it may split into sub-tasks, gets estimated with planning poker, and may depend on other stories. Stories accumulate in the Product Backlog, which the lecture notes is like a WBS except it evolves — fixed upfront versus growing throughout the project. User-story common sense, per the slides: stories are about users, the people who will actually use the software — never write 'as a database' or 'as a system'.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: Two parts is a fail: role + want without benefit (or any missing third) loses marks.
System internals are not stories: 'as a developer, I want clean code' is a task, not a user story.
One story, one goal: stuffing two functionalities into one sentence breaks estimation and backlog ordering.

callout.text: 2022 Q2.1 marking logic: 1 mark per part explained (role/want/benefit), then 2 marks per story (1 for a valid three-part sentence, 1 for a distinct, sensible railway functionality). Write exactly two stories — a third cannot earn, but can confuse.

summary: User stories say As a <role> I want <goal> so that <benefit> — one sentence, all three parts, written for real users, estimated and backlogged like any task.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: The flow of events (FoE) narrates the happy-days scenario: actor does something, system responds, repeat until the goal is achieved. Extensions handle everything else. Together they carry 10 of the 2022 paper's 25 requirements marks — the most heavily rewarded writing in the midterm.

sections.heading: Writing the main flow
paras: As a rough guide, the FoE runs about half a dozen steps (the lecture gives an explicit size steer): alternate actor action and system response, number each step, keep the system inside its scope. The Uploading-a-Video example opens '1. The uploader chooses a file to upload. 2. ...' — concrete, observable, no implementation detail.

Things to avoid, per the slides: don't narrate interactions between two actors (the system must mediate), don't describe things outside the system's scope, and don't drown the flow in UI minutiae. 'What about IF statements' gets its own slide: branching logic belongs in extensions, not embedded conditionals in the main flow.

sections.heading: Writing extensions
paras: Each extension has an ID like 4B: the step where it diverges plus a letter, so the reader can locate the branch point. Structure: condition (what went differently), handling (what the system does), outcome (where the flow resumes, or that the use case aborts). The worked example 2A — 'the uploaded file is not a valid video file' — shows the pattern: detect, inform, offer recovery, resume or end.

For the 2022 plotting scenario, strong extensions write themselves from the description: non-numeric data (prompt to proceed with valid data only), no save privileges (prompt access-right elevation; abort if refused), no datasets for the user's credentials. Each earns marks by naming the step, the system's exact behaviour, and the resume point.
Avoid overly-generic problems — the slides' exhibit A is 'database network connection fails'. Extensions should be use-case-specific failures a designer can actually handle, not acts of God.

callout.text: 2022 Q2.2(b) flow [5]: one mark per sensible step up to five — alternate actor/system, cover login, dataset listing, column/chart/colour selection, generation + save. summary: Main flow narrates happy days in numbered actor-system steps; extensions branch by ID with condition, handling and outcome — scenario-specific, never generic.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: A UML use-case diagram shows the names of all use cases, all actors, and which actors participate in which use cases — a map of scope, not a story. The lecture is unusually frank: use-case diagrams have limited usefulness next to written descriptions. They show who is involved in what; the description carries the actual requirements.

sections.heading: The vocabulary
paras: Ovals are use cases at task level (Watch Video, Upload Video, Report Video in the running video-sharing example). Stick figures are actors; lines (associations) show participation — the 'who does what' view. The include relationship factors out a shared sub-flow used by several cases (dashed arrow toward the included case): one 'Authenticate User' included by many cases beats five copies. sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Non-functional requirements say what the system should be: fast, reliable, usable, secure — the characteristics of functions rather than the functions themselves. The lecture opens with the gap: 'print' alone is not a requirement until you know how fast, how reliably, and measurably how. NFRs close that gap, and the unit tests them harder than any other requirements topic.

sections.heading: Core explanation
paras: NFRs mostly end in '-ility': usability, security, reliability, and friends. They typically start with 'The system shall...' and attach measurable bounds. They can be listed alongside particular use cases, or held as system-wide constraints in backlogs — but there is no such thing as a purely non-functional use case: a use case as a whole represents a functional requirement.

The worksheet's recognition test is the one to internalise: (1) from the user's point of view, is this a function or a characteristic of a function? (2) Could I write a use-case flow-of-events for it? If you can write the flow, it is functional. If it constrains the flow's qualities, it is non-functional. Then the kicker: 'How could I test it? If you can't test it, it's not valid.'

sections.heading: Why specify NFRs
paras: Because qualities left unspecified get whatever the developers felt like: the lecture's 'for non-superheroes' argument is that ordinary users need guaranteed responsiveness, availability and learnability, not heroic patience. The Gephi SRS shows the professional end-state: performance requirements quantified against a 500 MHz CPU and 128 MB RAM baseline.

summary: NFRs name the system's qualities — testable characteristics of functions, never functions themselves, with no such thing as a purely non-functional use case.

paras: (a) 'System must allow students to see available courses and timetable' — invalid because it is functional: from the user's view it is a function, and you could write its flow of events. It may be a fine requirement, but it is miscategorised, and miscategorised requirements escape the measurability discipline NFRs demand.

(b) '...in user friendly manner' — invalid twice over: 'user friendly' is ambiguous (no two markers picture the same threshold) and hence unverifiable (no observation decides pass/fail). The rewrite (Q3.3) must convert friendliness into a measurable usability requirement: pick a user task, a time or effort bound, and a success criterion — e.g. 'An average new user shall locate and display any available ticket type within 60 seconds of first seeing the catalogue, unaided, with at least 9 of 10 succeeding.'

paras: Item (d) 'must support images up to 100 megapixels' is a capacity characteristic — valid if bounded and testable. Item (e) 'colour enhance within 250 ms on a 10 MP image on an average PC' is the gold-standard shape: operation, bound, workload, environment. Items (h) 'suitable for inclusion in a photo album' and (j) 'must take over 1 minute to open' fail ambiguity and perversity checks respectively. Item (f) crash-rate-per-1000-hours is valid reliability if the failure class and observation method are defined.

summary: Valid NFRs are unambiguous, doable, verifiable, in-scope and truly non-functional — testable constraints, never disguised functions or vibes.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Performance is software speed under stated conditions — and conditions are half the requirement. Overall performance is as much due to hardware as software, so a bound without an environment ('fast on average PCs' vs 'fast on the ward tablet') is untestable. The 2022 paper's patient-monitor question rewards students who pin all four parts down.

sections.heading: The four-part shape
paras: Operation (what is timed: colour-enhance, chart generation, vital-sign refresh), bound (250 ms, 2 s), workload (10 MP image, 50 concurrent plots), environment (average PC, ward tablet, specified CPU/RAM as in the Gephi SRS). The worksheet's model specimen — 'the colour enhance function shall take at most 250 ms to enhance a 10 MP image on an average PC' — passes every validity property precisely because all four are present.

For the 2022 patient monitor: 'The system shall refresh displayed oxygen level and blood pressure at least once every 2 seconds during continuous monitoring on the ward tablet' — operation, bound, workload, environment, and safety-relevant (stale vitals mislead clinicians).

sections.heading: Testing: stochastic reality
paras: Timing measurements are stochastic: repeated runs give a scatter (#1-#5 in the slides), so verification needs repeated observation and a statistical rule (mean, percentile, worst-of-N) stated in advance — otherwise 'maybe' verdicts return. Fix the hardware, warm the caches, state the percentile: that is what turns a speed wish into a verifiable requirement.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
bullets: 'As fast as possible' is not a requirement: no bound, no test.
Single-run timing proves nothing: stochastic measurements need repetitions.
Hardware excuses cut both ways: if the environment is unspecified, the requirement — not the code — is at fault.

summary: Performance requirements bind an operation, a time bound, a workload and an environment — then verify with repeated, statistically-ruled measurement.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Usability requirements state what users must be able to do with the system — within a time, or with an effort — thanks to how the system is built. The UI (the part of the system users touch) is where most usability lives, and the lecture offers two measurement approaches: count what users achieve (task success, time-on-task) or assess interface characteristics against principles. Either way, the requirement ends in numbers.

sections.heading: The formula + the trap
paras: User class (average new user, trained cashier) + task (rotate a photo to within 3 degrees of level, locate a ticket type) + bound (within 20 seconds, unaided) + success criterion (9 of 10 succeeding). The worksheet's star specimen: 'an average user must be able, within 20 seconds, to rotate a tilted photograph so that it is within 3 degrees of level.'

The trap is business rules in disguise. 'The user is required to enter a password' constrains the user — a rule. 'An average user shall be able to log in within 30 seconds unaided' describes what the system enables — a usability requirement. The 2019 restaurant usability answer must enable (order a meal within N minutes unaided), never obligate.

sections.heading: Worked answers
paras: 2019 restaurant: 'An average first-time customer shall complete a standard order and card payment within 5 minutes of pressing start, unaided, with at least 9 of 10 succeeding in evaluation.' 2022 ticketing rewrite: same shape, ticket-type task. Both name the user class (average/first-time), the task, the bound, and the bar — which is exactly the hidden mark scheme.

summary: Usability requirements quantify what defined users can achieve within what time or effort — system-enabled ability, never user obligations.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Beyond the big three (performance, reliability, usability) sit security, interoperability, localisation and accessibility — each with its own lecture slide and a standing invitation in Worksheet 4 Q5. sections.heading: The four, briefly
bullets: Security — everyone's responsibility: authentication, authorisation, audit. Vitals are health data; unauthorised display or alteration harms patients.

Localisation (L10N) — adapt language, units, culture: ward staff across campuses need consistent units and terminology.
Accessibility — cater for diverse abilities: alarms perceivable by staff with hearing or vision limits; operable gloved and one-handed.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: The Software Requirements Specification is the document listing all requirements — and IEEE 830 is the standard describing what a good one looks like. The lecture lifts its layout wholesale (introduction, overall description, interfaces, functional requirements, NFRs), and the Gephi SRS shows a real one in the wild. Midterm questions rarely ask IEEE by name, but every 'write a valid requirement' mark is secretly graded against it.

sections.heading: A good SRS (IEEE 4.3)
paras: Correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked for importance/stability, verifiable, modifiable, traceable. Two of these do quiet exam work: ranked (not all requirements matter equally — the Product Backlog's ordering is ranking made agile) and traceable (each requirement linkable to its source and its tests — the ancestor of this wiki's citations). The standard's hall of shame for verifiability — 'works well', 'good human interface', 'shall usually happen' — is the same family as the lecture's 'user friendly' and the worksheet's 'suitable for photo albums'. Learn to hear the register: unmeasurable adjectives are failed requirements.

sections.heading: Layout you should recognise

The Gephi SRS follows this skeleton across 37 pages — skim its table of contents once and the abstract standard becomes concrete.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Ethics is personal, cultural, ideological — about how human beings, not just software, can come to harm. The unit opens the topic with moral philosophy because software engineers hold power over people they will never meet, and power without a framework for right and wrong is just luck. The midterm tests this as reasoning, not recitation: Worksheet 5 asks for stories, not slogans.

paras: The handout's map (Figure 1) splits consequentialism into utilitarianism, then rule vs act utilitarianism, set against deontology's rule list. Utilitarianism answers deontology's rigidity — rules collide, and strict obedience can mandate cruelty — provided you can define and measure 'utility', which is itself contested. Neither school wins; the unit's point is that you can now name the disagreement instead of waving at it.

sections.heading: The trolley problem
paras: An out-of-control tram will kill five people tied to the tracks; you can pull a lever to divert it, killing one person instead. The lecture uses it to show that moral principles and their practical integration differ — knowing the theory does not dissolve the dilemma, it structures your deliberation about it. In software terms: every 'move fast' shortcut is a small trolley decision about other people's safety, privacy and livelihoods.

summary: Moral philosophy gives engineers two lenses — duty to rules vs outcomes for the many — whose honest disagreement (see: trolley) is the start of ethical deliberation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Software exists in society and impacts society: your code decides who sees what, who gets paid, who is watched. The lecture's core claim is leverage — with the profession comes power, and with power comes responsibility, because every good act is amplified by deployment and every mistake is amplified with it. Professionalism is the discipline of wielding that leverage properly.

sections.heading: Areas of concern
paras: Harms the public can suffer from your work (the lecture's Examples 1-2 plus the handout's scenarios): planning-poker estimates falsified under client pressure; social-media features shipped per-sprint without considering harassment or surveillance consequences; platform power used to crush dependent app businesses; facial or welfare systems whose extensions reject valid names and deny people payments. Worksheet 5's method — come up with reasons people behave unethically, then write harm stories for given systems and present them for critique — trains exactly this imagination: who is harmed, how, and what would you have done differently?

Counterbalancing goods matter too: the same power builds tools for the good life (access, knowledge, coordination) when engineers identify stakeholders honestly and protect the public as their primary obligation.

sections.heading: Professionalism and codes
paras: Professionalism is essentially doing the job properly — competence, honesty, care — and codes of conduct from professional bodies (ACS, IEEE-CS) remind engineers what 'properly' means. The ACS Code is explicit: membership of a profession means abiding by its code; where cases are ambiguous, apply the spirit of the Code; public interest (health, safety, environment) takes in all affected people; and stakeholder trust underlies every decision. The IEEE-CS short code and ACS rules sit side by side in the slides: know that both exist, what values they share (public safety first, honesty, competence), and that neither is optional decoration.

summary: Software leverage amplifies good and harm alike; professionalism means competence plus honesty guided by codes that put public safety and stakeholder trust first.

sections.heading: The shape of the midterm
paras: The 2022 paper (90 minutes, 100 marks, closed book, four questions of 25) is the best predictor available: Q1 planning (waterfall + full network analysis + management use), Q2 functional requirements (stories + a complete use case with flow, extension and task goals), Q3 FR/NFR (distinctions, demolitions, usability rewrite, quantified performance/reliability/other NFRs), Q4 agile (burn-up arithmetic, Kanban reasoning, Scrum backlogs and events). Earlier papers add AOA graphs (2018), restaurant ordering cases (2019), plus testing and version-control questions from topics outside the current lecture set.

sections.heading: Where to start reading
bullets: First: Critical path and slack (highest mark density), Use-case flow (most writing marks), NFR validity (most conceptual marks).
Second: Burn-up charts, Scrum events and backlogs, User stories, Activity graphs.
Third: Ethics theories + professionalism (reasoning marks), SRS/IEEE 830 (background that sharpens every requirement answer).
Drills: 2018 AON/AOA + add-friend case; 2019 restaurant case + NFR set; 2022 full paper under timed conditions.

recall.a: Slogans without stakeholders, harm, framework or code; confusing the two schools; treating codes as decoration rather than action-guiding.
recall.q: What makes an ethics answer score poorly?

sections.heading: How ethics marks are lost
bullets: Declaring an action 'unethical' without naming stakeholders or harm.
Summarising deontology/utilitarianism without applying either to the scenario.
Citing codes of conduct without saying what action they require.
Harm stories with no lapse identified and no preventive alternative.

summary: Ethics mark-losers: slogans instead of stakeholder-harm-framework-code-action structure.
title: Ethics: common exam mistakes
